question.prompt: Orvin went to the store with just enough money to buy \(30\) balloons. When he arrived, he discovered that the store had a special sale on balloons: buy \(1\) balloon at the regular price and get a second at \(\frac{1}{3}\) off the regular price. What is the greatest number of balloons Orvin could buy?

solutions.explanation:
Use the positive regular price of one balloon as the unit of money. Orvin's budget is then \(30\) units. A discount of \(\frac13\) off means the second balloon costs \(\frac23\) of its regular price, so a sale pair costs
\[
1+\frac23=\frac53
\]
units. His budget buys
\[
30\div\frac53=18
\]
pairs, giving \(18\cdot2=36\) balloons.

To prove this is the maximum, pair each discounted balloon with the full-price balloon required for its discount. Each pair costs \(\frac56\) unit per balloon, while any unpaired balloon costs \(1\) unit. Therefore any purchase of \(37\) or more balloons costs at least
\[
37\cdot\frac56=\frac{185}{6}>30
\]
units. Since \(36\) balloons are affordable and every larger number is not, the answer is \(36\), choice C.
solutions.title: Buy sale pairs and prove the maximum
